community-s9c.u1-emuA:
One thing that struck me about the way they approach leadership is this idea of mandar obedeciendo: leading by obeying. Basically, the representatives have to do what the assembly tells them to, and are accountable to the people.

Another thing that’s striking about the Zapatistas is that they’re the closest I’ve seen to an entire example of what I’ve been talking about. Not only do they have autonomous voting, but also education, health care, justice, collective production, political training, etc. They’re also developing ways to teach others and are coordinating beyond the village level.
community-s9c.u1-emuB:
This is super, super impressive. Part of this is mandar obedeciendo, leading by obeying, because the reps are supposed to do what the assembly says and be accountable to them.

And this is the closest I’ve seen to a whole example, because they do a lot more than voting. They have their own education, health, justice, collective production, political training, ways of teaching outsiders, etc., and coordinate beyond the village.
community-s9c.u1:
What impressed me most was how they handle authority, with the principle of mandar obedeciendo, or leading by obeying. Their representatives carry out what the assembly decided, and they stay answerable to the people who gave them the mandate.

The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because their autonomy goes beyond how they vote. They've set up their own education and health care, and their own justice. They run their own collective production and political training. They've also worked out their own ways of teaching outsiders, all while coordinating beyond a single village.
community-s9c.u2-emuA: As most institutions age, they become more bureaucratic. The Zapatistas conducted a review and simplified their organizational structure by devolving authority. And contrary to the many leadership gurus, they didn’t write a book about it and then certify others to teach it, they actually did it.
community-s9c.u2-emuB: The pattern in most institutions is that as they age they become more bureaucratic. The Zapatistas deliberately reviewed their institutional structure, and rather than adding more offices, they decided to shift authority downward. They didn’t just write a book on how to do it, and they didn’t create a certification program for people to learn how to do it, they just changed the way their own system worked.
community-s9c.u2: Most institutions pile up layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas reviewed theirs and moved authority down. They didn't write a book on leadership and start a certification program. They actually changed the system they were living in.
community-s9c.u3-emuA: Maybe one of the only aspects of the Zapatistas that could be copied, is their own willingness to constantly change their own structures based on real, lived experience. As they've openly said: do not import/export Zapatismo, but learn to learn from what they're doing. As they say, they learn by doing and if it doesn't work, they change their structures.
community-s9c.u3-emuB: One thing the Zapatistas have been very clear about is that people shouldn’t import or export Zapatismo. It’s ok to copy how the Zapatistas learn, though. In other words, learn through building. Learn through figuring things out. When something isn’t working the way it’s supposed to work, change the structure.
community-s9c.u3: They've warned people themselves not to import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. What's worth copying is how they learn. They build something and ask questions. They find out where the practice fails, and then they change the structure.
community-s9c.u4-emuA: This doesn't prove that the entire path I'm arguing for, of making internal necessities non-priced, and moving to a common purse to get rid of outside money altogether, is the way to go. The Zapatistas still work together in common to provide for schools and clinics and a functioning autonomous government and to fight off the scum that would oppress them. They still sell and trade. They still get some support from the outside world. But it proves that it is possible to remove the great bulk of necessities and public functions from the market and take them in hand collectively. It proves that it is possible to receive outside aid in a way that builds capabilities, rather than creating gatekeepers and uneven dependence.
community-s9c.u4-emuB: Though this does not prove my whole theory, it does show that part of the path I posit for a better economy- moving internal necessities off of the market- is possible. It is also an example of some of the benefits of moving towards a more common purse for a group. In this case, the Zapatistas are pooling their work to provide not only for themselves, but also for their infrastructure of schools, clinics, government, and resistance. It is also interesting to note that the Zapatistas are not completely off of the outside economy- they still sell, trade, and recieve support from the outside world. My theory ultimately intends to get rid of the outside money, but I still see possible benefits of outside support, as it seems to help the Zapatistas be more capable. However, I also see ways that this outside support could be seen as problematic- who is giving it and why? It may lead to unequal relationships and dependancy on outside agents, which may act as gatekeepers.
community-s9c.u4: They also don't prove my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities to a common purse to getting rid of outside money. Zapatista communities pool their work to support their schools and clinics, their autonomous government and their resistance. They also sell things and trade, and they get support from outside. What they do show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken off the market and run collectively. Outside help can build capability. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, when the specialist, the donor or the organization stays indispensable.
community-s9c.u5-emuA:
To celebrate the 10 anniversary of their autonomous governments, the zapatistas organised a set of escuelitas, where outsiders could live with their families and learn about their processes of constructing autonomy. While only 1500 people went for the first set of escuelitas, in the latest thousands went.

A way the escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business in which people’s lives are a performance of community life for paying outsiders, and its success is measured in how many people come, rather than how many daughter communities are started. It is not primarily about providing a week of transformative experience for people to go and tell their friends about, but about teaching people enough about how the social and material system works for some of them to be able to put one together.
community-s9c.u5-emuB:
One of the ways that the Zapatistas celebrated their ten years of building autonomous governments was to open “escuelitas” – little schools – where outsiders could come and stay with families and learn how this was done. There were around 1500 students for the first escuelita, and thousands for subsequent ones.

One of the ways that an escuelita can fail is when it falls into the trap of becoming like a business that profits off of visitors. Then the people of the community are performing community for the benefit of the paying customers, and they measure the success of their escuelita by the number of people they’ve made feel transformed for a week, rather than the number of daughter communities they’ve helped to spin off with enough knowledge of the social and material system to build it in a new place.
community-s9c.u5:
To celebrate ten years of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened the Escuelita. Outsiders came to stay with families, and they learned autonomy by taking part in daily life there. About 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to the later ones.

One way an escuelita can fail is by turning into a visitor business. Then the residents spend their lives putting on a show of community for outsiders who pay, and success gets measured by how many guests come instead of how many daughter communities get started. It shouldn't be about making people feel transformed for a week. It should teach enough of the social and material system that some of them can build it somewhere else.
community-s9c.u6-emuA: I looked for what I could. Yes, there are attempts to network with the people who went to the Escuelita and to take the practice home with them, and some later attempts at organizing. But to my knowledge, there is no research that links, for instance, attendance at the Escuelita with a greater likelihood of forming some new commmunal institution, or the relative success of people and their kids who have adopted some of these institutions. The Zapatistas were inspiring people internationally before they held the Escuelita. So, even if people’s practice ends up looking similar, it’s hard to say it’s because of the Escuelita. So I’m borrowing not just their practice, but their ambition to see it replicated.
community-s9c.u6-emuB: Part of what I’m looking for in this research is to see if there are any studies that establish a link between going to an Escuelita and people going home and setting up their own communal institutions and then looking at how those people and their kids did relative to others. I am sure that there are networks of people who went, who brought back the practice with them, and who have done some organizing, but I don’t know if anyone has found the link. The Zapatistas were inspiring people all over the world before the Escuelita, so I’m trying to borrow their inspiration, their teaching method, and their attempt to replicate when possible, but not borrow their proof.
community-s9c.u6: I also tried, in my research, to trace what came out of the Escuelita. I found alumni networks and people taking practices home, and there was organizing later on. What I couldn't find was a clear line from someone attending the Escuelita to a newly founded communal institution, along with evidence of how that institution's members and their kids actually did over time. The Zapatistas were already influencing people internationally before the Escuelita existed, so a later resemblance doesn't prove it came from there. I'm borrowing their way of teaching and their ambition to replicate, without claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.
community-s9c.u7-emuA: It’s interesting that Sociocracy, coming from a different history, arrived at many of the same forms. If there’s something to be harnessed in circles, consent, distributed authority, and linked levels, then it’s something all of use can benefit from knowing more about, even if it’s not a “universal formula”. At the very least, it’s a great system for people to be aware of, when embarking on community building.
community-s9c.u7-emuB: Sociocracy is interesting because it has a very different history, but it has landed on a similar form to what’s described here. Sociocracy uses circles, consent-based decision making, distributed authority, and a linking mechanism to connect the circles. It doesn’t prove that this system is a universal formula, but it’s worth learning about if/when communities want to build a system like this.
community-s9c.u7: Sociocracy arrived at some similar forms from a very different history. It works with circles and consent. It distributes authority and links its levels together. That resemblance doesn't prove there's a universal formula. But it gives people building a community another serious system to study, so they don't have to invent their governance in the middle of their first dispute.
